outline.description: Identify the court, parties, procedural setting, and disposition of the appeal. Frame the case as a Fifth Circuit review of a district court’s dismissal of a securities-fraud indictment arising from an alleged social-media-driven pump-and-dump scheme.
key_points: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

Parties: United States of America (plaintiff-appellant) v. Edward Constantinescu, Perry “PJ” Matlock, John Rybarczyk, Gary Deel, Stefan Hrvatin, Tom Cooperman, Mitchell Hennessey, and Daniel Knight (defendants-appellees below, except Knight pleaded guilty).
Appeal from the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas.
Charges at issue: conspiracy to commit securities fraud under 18 U.S.C. § 1349 and substantive securities fraud under 18 U.S.C. §§ 1348 and 2.
Panel: Higginson, Willett, and Engelhardt, Circuit Judges; opinion by Judge Engelhardt.
Disposition: Fifth Circuit reversed the district court’s dismissal of the indictment and remanded.
Core appellate question: whether the superseding indictment adequately alleged a scheme and intent to defraud after Ciminelli and in light of Kousisis.

outline.description: Set out the alleged pump-and-dump scheme, the defendants’ use of social media, the content of the indictment, and the procedural path to the Fifth Circuit. Emphasize that at the motion-to-dismiss stage the indictment’s allegations are taken as true.
key_points: The government alleged that defendants were prominent social-media stock traders with large followings across various platforms.
Defendants allegedly portrayed themselves as skilled traders and regularly posted about their trading activity.

According to the indictment, defendants executed a classic “pump and dump” scheme: they first bought securities, then “pumped” the stock by posting false and misleading information to induce followers to buy, thereby artificially inflating the price, and then “dumped” by secretly selling at a profit.
The indictment alleged that defendants misrepresented their trading positions and the future prospects or price potential of securities.
The government claimed defendants earned approximately $114 million from the alleged scheme.
The superseding indictment charged conspiracy to commit securities fraud and multiple substantive counts of securities fraud.
Defendant Knight pleaded guilty; the remaining defendants moved to dismiss the indictment.
The district court dismissed, reasoning that the indictment alleged only deprivation of potentially valuable economic information rather than a traditional property interest.
The government appealed the dismissal.
On appeal, the sufficiency of the indictment was reviewed de novo, and the allegations had to be accepted as true.

outline.description: State the legal questions the Fifth Circuit resolved concerning the sufficiency of the indictment under the federal securities-fraud statute, especially in light of Supreme Court precedent limiting fraud theories based on non-property interests.
key_points: Whether an indictment under 18 U.S.C. § 1348 sufficiently alleges a “scheme to defraud” when it claims defendants used material misrepresentations to induce social-media followers to purchase securities, thereby parting with money, rather than merely depriving them of valuable economic information.

Whether, after Ciminelli v. United States, the indictment improperly relied on a forbidden right-to-control theory or instead permissibly alleged a fraudulent-inducement theory targeting money or property.

Whether the indictment sufficiently alleged “intent to defraud” when defendants allegedly sought to profit from inducing purchases, even if the victims may have received market-value securities and even if the indictment did not allege intended net pecuniary loss to victims.

More broadly, whether a fraud indictment requires allegations that defendants intended to cause traditional economic loss, or whether it is enough that obtaining victims’ money or property by deception was an object of the scheme.

outline.description: Provide the court’s answers to each issue in clear, doctrinally precise terms.
key_points: Yes. The indictment sufficiently alleged a scheme to defraud because it charged that defendants used false and misleading statements to induce followers to purchase securities, causing them to part with money or property.
No. The indictment did not rest on the right-to-control theory rejected in Ciminelli; instead, it alleged a valid fraudulent-inducement theory recognized by the Supreme Court in Kousisis.

Yes. The indictment sufficiently alleged intent to defraud because it charged that defendants intended to obtain money through deception; the fraud statutes do not require that defendants intended to leave victims economically worse off.
The Fifth Circuit held that the indictment stated offenses under the securities-fraud statute and that the district court erred in dismissing it.
Result: reversal and remand for further proceedings.

outline.description: Explain in detail how the Fifth Circuit analyzed indictment sufficiency, interpreted § 1348 using mail- and wire-fraud principles, distinguished forbidden right-to-control theories from permissible fraudulent-inducement theories, and rejected the argument that intended victim loss is necessary. This should be the most developed section of the brief.
key_points: Standard of review: The court reviewed the sufficiency of the indictment de novo.
At the indictment stage, courts must accept the indictment’s factual allegations as true and ask only whether an offense has been stated.
An indictment is sufficient if it alleges each material element of the offense, fairly informs the defendant of the charges, and enables a future double-jeopardy defense.

The court noted that there is limited Fifth Circuit precedent interpreting 18 U.S.C. § 1348, but the statute borrows key concepts from the mail and wire fraud statutes, so those doctrines inform analysis.
Under Fifth Circuit precedent, securities fraud under § 1348 requires (1) a scheme to defraud and (2) intent to defraud.
A “scheme to defraud” requires a material misrepresentation intended to deceive others in order to obtain something of value, such as money, from the entity or person deceived.
“Intent to defraud” requires intent to deceive and intent to cause some harm from the deceit, but the court clarified this in light of the Supreme Court’s recent fraud cases.
The court relied heavily on Ciminelli v. United States and Kousisis v. United States to define the limits and scope of property fraud.

In Ciminelli, the Supreme Court rejected the right-to-control theory, which treated deprivation of potentially valuable economic information needed for discretionary economic decision-making as the relevant property interest.
The Fifth Circuit emphasized that, under Ciminelli, federal fraud statutes protect only traditional property interests, and valuable economic information alone is not such an interest.
The defendants argued that the indictment here was effectively a right-to-control case because it was based on followers being deprived of truthful information needed to decide whether to trade.

The Fifth Circuit rejected that framing because the indictment did not stop at alleging deception affecting decision-making; it alleged that defendants induced followers to purchase securities, meaning followers parted with money or property.
That allegation fits the fraudulent-inducement theory: a defendant uses material misstatements to trick a victim into a transaction requiring transfer of money or property.

The court treated fraudulent inducement as categorically different from right-to-control because the former directly targets money or property, while the latter targets informational autonomy divorced from traditional property.
Kousisis, decided after the district court’s dismissal, expressly confirmed that fraudulent-inducement theory is not simply a repackaged right-to-control theory.
Applying Kousisis, the Fifth Circuit concluded that the indictment alleged a property-based fraud because the object of the alleged deception was to cause followers to spend money to buy securities.
Thus, the indictment adequately alleged the “scheme to defraud” element.
On intent, defendants argued that the indictment failed because it showed only an intent to profit, not an intent to harm followers.
The court rejected this argument by relying on Kousisis’s holding that fraud statutes do not require intended or actual net economic loss to the victim.

Kousisis explained that a defendant violates the fraud statutes by scheming to obtain the victim’s money or property, regardless of whether the defendant seeks to leave the victim economically worse off.

The Fifth Circuit therefore held that even if followers received securities worth what they paid at the moment of purchase, the fraud was complete if they were induced by material falsehoods to part with their money.
The court reasoned that obtaining profit through deception and causing the victim to transfer money under false pretenses are legally sufficient to show fraudulent intent.

The distinction defendants tried to draw between intending to profit and intending to harm was “a distinction without a difference” because the object of the scheme was to obtain victims’ money by deceit.

The indictment specifically alleged that defendants posted false and misleading statements so other investors would buy the securities; this directly alleged both deception and the objective of obtaining money.
The court quoted Kousisis’s idea that the allegations showed defendants “had money in mind,” which is enough for property fraud.

The court further stressed that a fraud is complete once the defendant induces the deprivation of money or property through materially false pretenses, without any requirement of a mirror-image loss or net pecuniary injury.
The Fifth Circuit also cited prior circuit authority rejecting a strict requirement that the victim’s loss mirror the defendant’s gain.
Accordingly, the indictment sufficiently alleged both the scheme and intent elements of securities fraud, making dismissal improper.
Because the legal deficiency identified by the district court was incorrect, the Fifth Circuit reversed and remanded for ordinary criminal proceedings.

outline.description: Extract the legal principles the case applied or clarified, especially those governing § 1348 indictments, the property requirement in fraud cases, and the role of fraudulent inducement after Ciminelli and Kousisis.
key_points: An indictment is sufficient if it alleges each material element of the charged offense, fairly informs the defendant of the charges, and provides protection against double jeopardy.
On a motion to dismiss an indictment, courts accept the indictment’s factual allegations as true and determine only whether an offense has been stated.
Securities fraud under 18 U.S.C. § 1348 requires a scheme to defraud and intent to defraud.
Because § 1348 borrows key concepts from the mail and wire fraud statutes, courts may look to mail- and wire-fraud doctrine to interpret it.
Federal fraud statutes protect traditional property interests, not a freestanding right to accurate or valuable economic information for decision-making.
Under Ciminelli, a right-to-control theory based solely on deprivation of potentially valuable economic information cannot support a fraud conviction.
A fraudulent-inducement theory is valid where a defendant uses material misstatements to induce a victim to enter a transaction that transfers money or property.
Under Kousisis, fraudulent inducement is not a repackaging of the forbidden right-to-control theory because it directly protects money and property.
Fraud statutes do not require the government to allege or prove that the defendant intended to cause, or actually caused, net pecuniary loss to the victim.
It is sufficient that obtaining the victim’s money or property through deception was an object of the scheme.
A defendant’s intent to profit by inducing victims to part with money through materially false pretenses can satisfy intent to defraud even if victims received something of value in return.

outline.description: Note whether any judge wrote separately and summarize any separate opinions if they exist.
key_points: There was no concurrence or dissent noted in the opinion.
The panel decision appears to be unanimous.
The opinion was authored by Judge Engelhardt for the court.

outline.description: Explain why this case matters for securities-fraud doctrine, charging practice, and the post-Ciminelli landscape. Highlight its importance for distinguishing permissible property-fraud theories from impermissible information-deprivation theories.
key_points: The case is an important Fifth Circuit application of Ciminelli and Kousisis in the securities-fraud context.
It clarifies that social-media-based pump-and-dump allegations can state securities-fraud offenses when the indictment alleges that misrepresentations induced investors to spend money on securities.
The decision narrows defendants’ ability to recast fraudulent-inducement prosecutions as forbidden right-to-control cases merely because misinformation influenced investors’ choices.
It confirms that, in federal fraud law, the critical inquiry is whether money or property was the object of the deception, not whether victims ultimately suffered a net financial loss.
The opinion reinforces that securities-fraud indictments under § 1348 may be analyzed using mail- and wire-fraud principles.
For prosecutors, the case provides a roadmap for pleading fraud post-Ciminelli: allege concrete deprivation of money or property, not merely denial of truthful information.
For defense counsel, the case marks the limit of Ciminelli’s reach and signals that arguments based solely on absence of intended pecuniary harm may fail after Kousisis.
Doctrinally, the case helps distinguish informational harm from property harm in modern market-manipulation and online-investment-fraud prosecutions.
Practically, it supports continued use of § 1348 against pump-and-dump schemes conducted through social media and influencer-style trading channels.
